'''Knowles Ronald Kerry''' is an Australian biochemist and marine biologist known for his work in [[Antarctica]], considered the 'father' of the Marine Biology program of the [[Australian Antarctic Division]]. He held positions including Principal Research Scientist and expedition leader with the [[Australian National Antarctic Research Expeditions]] (ANARE) including seven total years in Antarctica and sub-Antarctic regions.<ref name="rchknowles">{{cite web |title=Alumni : Kerry, Knowles Ronald AAM |url=https://www.rch.org.au/alumni/alumni_profiles/Kerry,_Knowles_Ronald_AAM/ |website=www.rch.org.au |publisher=Royal Children's Hospital |access-date=13 July 2026}}</ref><ref name="aad-data-kerry-island">{{cite web |title=Kerry Island |url=https://data.aad.gov.au/aadc/gaz/display_name.cfm?gaz_id=136799 |website=data.aad.gov.au |publisher=Australian Antarctic Data Centre |access-date=13 July 2026}}</ref>

==Career==
Knowles Kerry began his career as a biochemist in the Gastroenterological Research Unit of the [[Royal Children's Hospital]] in [[Melbourne]]. <ref name="rchknowles" />

He embarked on his first of many expeditions to the Antarctic and sub-Antarctic after joining the [[Australian Antarctic Division]] (AAD), going to [[Macquarie Island]] in 1966.<ref name="amplify-interview">{{cite web |author1=McGaughey, Ingrid |title=Knowles Kerry interviewed by Ingrid McGaughey [Part 1] |url=https://amplify.gov.au/transcripts/statelibrarynsw/antarctic_expeditions/Antarctic_KnowlesKerry_Part1 |website=amplify.gov.au |publisher=State Library of New South Wales |access-date=13 July 2026 |language=en |date=10 August 2011}}</ref> He later spent winter for the first time on [[Macquarie Island]] researching seal milk and [[albatross]] birds, after undertaking earlier research on animals in the Southern Ocean.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kerry |first1=Knowles |title=Studies on the Behaviour and Reproduction of the Royal Penguin (Eudyptes chrysolophus schlegeli) - Macquarie Island 1967 |journal=Australian Antarctic Data Centre |date=1967 |url=https://data.aad.gov.au/metadata/Royal_Behaviour_Reproduction_Macca_1967 |access-date=13 July 2026}}</ref> This work was some of the first official scientific work other than [[physics]] by the Australian Government in Antarctica.<ref name="rchknowles" /> This early work led to Kerry being instrumental in establishing the Marine Biology program at the AAD.<ref name="aad-medal-knowles">{{cite web |title=Knowles Ronald Kerry – Antarctic Medal recipient 1993 – Australian Antarctic Program |url=https://www.antarctica.gov.au/about-antarctica/australia-in-antarctica/australian-antarctic-medal/recipients/knowles-ronald-kerry/ |website=www.antarctica.gov.au |publisher=Australian Antarctic Division |access-date=13 July 2026 |language=en |date=17 January 2013}}</ref>

Later in his career he was instrumental in negotiating the [[Convention on the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources]] (CCAMLR) to improve the management of fisheries in Antarctic waters. Kerry served as a member of the Australian delegation and scientific delegate.<ref name="rchknowles" />

Through the 1980s he commenced leading a key research program on krill availability in Antarctic waters focused on [[Adélie penguins]]. Part of this program involved a homemade device used to spray orange paint onto penguins to mark them for research, displayed in the [[National Museum of Australia]].<ref>{{cite web |title=National Museum of Australia - Handheld instruments |url=https://www.nma.gov.au/antarctica/explore-antarctica/handheld-instruments |website=www.nma.gov.au |publisher=National Museum of Australia |access-date=13 July 2026 |language=en}}</ref> This research culminated in its publication in 1990. The program continued with new technology including satellite tracking and depth recording. He continued further work on Adélie penguins and their behaviour, feeding habits and health for many decades.<ref name="rchknowles" /><ref>{{cite web |title=Dead Penguins |url=https://www.abc.net.au/listen/programs/radionational-breakfast/dead-penguins/3496230 |website=ABC Radio National Breakfast |publisher=Australian Broadcasting Corporation |access-date=13 July 2026 |language=en-AU |date=29 November 2001}}</ref>

Kerry was involved in several international programs of cooperation between Australia and other countries' Antarctic programs. In 1980 he was part of hosting the first research scientists from [[Chinese Arctic and Antarctic Administration|China]] to visit Antarctica at [[Casey Station]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Figure 1 Dong Zhaoqian (left), Dr. Knowles Kerry (middle) and Zhang... |url=https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Dong-Zhaoqian-left-Dr-Knowles-Kerry-middle-and-Zhang-Qingsong-right-near-the_fig1_313756935 |website=ResearchGate |access-date=13 July 2026 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="rchknowles" /> Between 1997 and 2006 he cooperated the Antarctic programs of [[National Antarctic Research Program|Italy]] at [[Zucchelli Station]] in [[Terra Nova Bay]] and the [[United States Antarctic Program|United States]] at [[McMurdo Station]].

==Awards and legacy==
In 1995. Kerry was awarded the Australian Antarctic Medal for his services to Antarctic science.<ref name="honours-aam-knowles-kerry">{{cite web |title=Australian Honours Search Facility |url=https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/899768 |website=honours.pmc.gov.au |publisher=Australian Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet |access-date=14 July 2026}}</ref>

Kerry Island, on the coast of mainland Antarctica, was named in his honour on 29 April 2009.<ref name="aad-data-kerry-island" />
